title: Classical hardness of approximate Boson Sampling
formal: Is the following classical sampling impossibility statement true? There is no single probabilistic classical Turing machine \(M\) and polynomial \(p\) such that, for every valid ideal Boson Sampling input \(B\) defined below and every integer \(k\ge2\), the machine \(M(B,1^k)\) outputs an occupation vector with law \(Q_{B,k}\), always halts in at most \(p(|B|+k)\) steps, and satisfies \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q_{B,k},D_B)=\frac12\sum_{s\in\Omega_{m,n}}|Q_{B,k}(s)-D_B(s)|\le\frac1k?\] The target distribution is \[D_B(s)=\frac{|\operatorname{Per}(A_s)|^2}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_j!},\qquad A=\operatorname{GS}(B),\qquad \Omega_{m,n}=\{s\in\mathbb N_0^m:\sum_js_j=n\}.\] Thus the approximation must meet every requested error tolerance, in time polynomial in the explicit network description and the inverse tolerance. The claim is unconditional and concerns all valid inputs, rather than only typical random optical networks.
why: This asks for an unconditional boundary between classical sampling and a concrete, restricted quantum optical experiment. It would clarify whether reproducing an entire physically defined distribution can require superpolynomial classical resources even when universal quantum computation is not part of the device model.

sentences: Boson Sampling records the occupations of indistinguishable photons after an ideal passive optical network.

The selected question asks whether no uniform classical randomized algorithm can reproduce every such distribution to any requested total-variation error in time polynomial in the input size and inverse error.
The distribution includes collisions and is defined by squared permanents with factorial normalization.
Known hierarchy-collapse consequences and newer average-case results have explicit assumptions or use different error guarantees.
An unconditional answer would establish or refute a fundamental classical limitation for a restricted quantum sampling experiment.

definitions:
There are \(n\ge1\) indistinguishable photons and \(m\ge n\) modes. A mode is one orthogonal single-particle state. Initially each of the first \(n\) modes contains one photon and every other mode is empty. The network is ideal passive linear optics: it preserves photon number and acts on the single-particle mode space by an \(m\times m\) unitary matrix \(U\). It has no loss, noise, distinguishability of photons, intermediate measurements, adaptive feed-forward or postselection. The output records the photon count in every mode. Collisions, meaning two or more photons in a mode, are included.

Only the first \(n\) columns of \(U\) matter for this input. Write these columns as \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}\), so \(A^\dagger A=I_n\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. Any such column isometry can be completed to a unitary, and the distribution below is independent of that completion. The input therefore specifies this part of the optical network rather than an exponentially large many-photon transition matrix.

Here is an explicit finite encoding of the matrix convention in the source's footnote19. The input \(B\) contains \(m,n\) and every entry of an \(m\times n\) complex matrix. Real and imaginary parts are signed dyadic rationals, each stored as an integer numerator and a nonnegative denominator exponent in unary: \(a/2^b\). All numerator bits, signs, exponents and matrix entries count toward \(|B|\). Dimensions and lists are explicitly delimited. A valid input satisfies \[\|B^\dagger B-I_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac12,\] where the operator norm is \(\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Cv\|_2\). This promise ensures that the columns are linearly independent. It is a convenient fixed conditioning threshold for the finite encoding, not a physical noise parameter. Define the represented ideal isometry by exact ordered Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization: for the columns \(b_j\) of \(B\), set \[v_j=b_j-\sum_{i<j}a_i(a_i^\dagger b_j),\qquad a_j=v_j/\sqrt{v_j^\dagger v_j},\] using the positive square root, and let \(A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). These equations define the ideal mathematical distribution exactly; they do not give the classical sampler a real-arithmetic oracle or make numerical computation free. Finer explicit dyadic approximations can represent arbitrary optical isometries to arbitrary precision. The encoding spells out the source's correction of a finite-precision matrix to an isometry; its chosen threshold does not impose a restriction on the number of photons or on network depth.

For \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\Omega_{m,n}\), form the square \(n\times n\) matrix \(A_s\) by repeating row \(j\) of \(A\) exactly \(s_j\) times, in increasing row order. For an \(n\times n\) matrix \(C\), its permanent is \[\operatorname{Per}(C)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i)},\] where \(S_n\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The factorial convention is \(0!=1\). The bosonic transition rule gives the displayed \(D_B\); because \(A\) is an isometry, these nonnegative probabilities sum to one. The output lists all \(m\) occupation numbers in binary. No requirement to enumerate the whole distribution or to estimate each exponentially small probability is imposed.

The classical machine is a uniform multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. It receives the complete explicit finite input, has no advice, quantum operations or oracle, and its polynomial runtime bound holds for every input and every random tape. Correctness is required only on valid matrices. For each such input, its output must lie in \(\Omega_{m,n}\). The law \(Q_{B,k}\) averages over all its random bits; there is no separate high-probability event certifying closeness. Total variation compares this full output law with the target distribution. The polynomial and machine are fixed independently of \(m,n,B,k\).

The unary accuracy input \(1^k\) requests error at most \(1/k\). This gives the arbitrary-error convention \(\varepsilon>0\) with runtime polynomial in input length and \(1/\varepsilon\): choose \(k=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\). It does not require polynomial dependence on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Every \(m\ge n\) is allowed, with its full matrix encoding charged; in particular the class includes the dilute, polynomially many-mode families used in the original hardness results. It does not claim that every individual network is hard. Easy subfamilies are compatible with the universal-sampler impossibility statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the impossibility statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation by a uniform classical probabilistic machine with one polynomial bound satisfying all input, output and accuracy quantifiers above. A positive answer must rule out every such machine without assuming a separation of complexity classes or an unproved permanent conjecture. A conditional polynomial-hierarchy consequence, hardness of computing an individual probability, an exact-sampling lower bound, a multiplicative-error result, a fixed numerical error guarantee, or experiments on finitely many networks do not settle this total-variation question. This is an exact yes/no question about arbitrarily requested sampling accuracy; the benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not replace its quantified error requirement.

context_blocks.text: The overview presents Boson Sampling as a restricted quantum experiment whose output distribution is conjectured to be difficult to reproduce classically. Its source paragraph does not choose an error model. On 16 September2026 the user selected approximate sampling to every requested total-variation error with polynomial inverse-error cost; this card records that specialization explicitly. The exact version remains distinct source context, not an asserted equivalent formulation.

Passive optics acts linearly on the single-photon modes, but the output probabilities for several indistinguishable photons involve squared permanents and factorial collision factors. Sampling asks for one random occupation pattern with the right distribution, rather than a list of all probabilities. The two computational tasks cannot be identified merely from that formula.

The 2013 paper proves that an efficient exact classical sampler would entail a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. Its route to a corresponding total-variation statement additionally uses conjectures about average-case Gaussian permanents and anticoncentration. These are conditional consequences; neither the noncollapse of the hierarchy nor all the required permanent statements are unconditional theorems.

The 2025 work substantially strengthens average-case probability-estimation hardness and proves a conditional multiplicative-error sampling theorem. Its Theorem1 still has an accuracy gap relative to the permanent conjecture, while Theorem3 assumes noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy and an anticoncentration conjecture. Multiplicative control of individual probabilities is stronger than the total-variation guarantee selected here.

The present claim concerns ideal indistinguishable photons and a sampler that works on every explicitly represented network. Typical-network hardness, constant-error hardness, loss-tolerant experiments and Gaussian Boson Sampling are separate variants. No measured experimental advantage or special family of classically simulable networks decides the stated universal-sampler question.
